title: Imports and Namespace
content: Imports $\texttt{Nat.Basic}$, $\texttt{Nat.Choose.Basic}$ for binomial coefficients $\binom{n}{k}$, $\texttt{Finset.Basic}$ for finite sets of points, and $\texttt{Tactic}$ for $\texttt{norm\_num}$ verification. The namespace $\texttt{Erdos503}$ scopes all definitions.
mathContext: The bounds involve $\binom{n+2}{2}$ and $\binom{n+1}{2}$, requiring $\texttt{Nat.choose}$. The abstract metric space uses $\texttt{Dist}$ for pairwise distance computation.

title: Isosceles Set Definition
content: A finite set $A$ in a metric space is an isosceles set if every triple of distinct points $\{x, y, z\} \subset A$ satisfies $d(x,y) = d(y,z)$ or $d(y,z) = d(x,z)$ or $d(x,y) = d(x,z)$—at least two of the three pairwise distances are equal. Equivalently, no triple forms a scalene triangle. The formalization uses an abstract $\texttt{Dist}$ typeclass rather than fixing $\mathbb{R}^n$.
mathContext:
$	exttt{IsIsoscelesSet}(A) \iff  orall x,y,z \in A,\; x 
eq y 
eq z 
eq x \Rightarrow d(x,y) = d(y,z) \lor d(y,z) = d(x,z) \lor d(x,y) = d(x,z)$. Three cases correspond to the three possible pairs of equal distances.

title: Maximum Isosceles Set Size $f(n)$
content: The extremal function $f(n) = \texttt{maxIsoscelesSize}(n)$: the largest cardinality of an isosceles set in $\mathbb{R}^n$. Axiomatized as a function $\mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ since the supremum exists (finite upper bound from Blokhuis). The problem: determine $f(n)$ for each $n$.
mathContext: $f(n) = \max\{|A| : A \subset \mathbb{R}^n,\; A \text{ is isosceles}\}$. Known: $f(1) = 3$ (trivial), $f(2) = 6$ (Kelly), $f(3) = 8$ (Croft). Unknown for $n \geq 4$.

title: Kelly's Theorem: $f(2) = 6$
content: L. M. Kelly proved (with Erdős, 1947) that the maximum isosceles set in the plane has exactly 6 points. The extremal configuration is the vertex set of a regular hexagon: every triple of vertices of a regular hexagon forms an isosceles triangle. An alternative proof was given by Kovács [Ko24c] using a case analysis on distance graphs.
mathContext: $f(2) = 6 = \binom{4}{2}$. The regular hexagon vertices $\{e^{2\pi i k/6} : k = 0, \ldots, 5\}$ achieve this. Note $\binom{3}{2} + 1 = 4 \leq 6 = \binom{4}{2}$, so the Blokhuis bound is tight for $n = 2$.

title: Croft's Theorem: $f(3) = 8$
content: H. T. Croft proved in 1962 that the maximum isosceles set in $\mathbb{R}^3$ has exactly 8 points. The extremal configuration uses vertices of specific polyhedra. The answer $f(3) = 8$ lies strictly between the general bounds: $\binom{4}{2}+1 = 7 \leq 8 \leq \binom{5}{2} = 10$.
mathContext: $f(3) = 8$. Compare: $\binom{4}{2}+1 = 7 < 8 < 10 = \binom{5}{2}$. Neither the Weisenberg lower bound nor the Blokhuis upper bound is tight for $n = 3$.

title: Blokhuis Upper Bound: $f(n) \leq \binom{n+2}{2}$
content: Aart Blokhuis proved in 1984 that any isosceles set in $\mathbb{R}^n$ has at most $\binom{n+2}{2} = \frac{(n+2)(n+1)}{2}$ points. The proof uses the dimension of the space of symmetric bilinear forms: associating to each point a distance profile in the $\binom{|A|}{2}$-dimensional space of pairwise distances, the isosceles condition forces linear dependencies.

title: Alweiss Lower Bound: $f(n) \geq \binom{n+1}{2}$
content: Ryan Alweiss constructed isosceles sets of size $\binom{n+1}{2}$ in $\mathbb{R}^n$ using the set of vectors $\{e_i + e_j : 1 \leq i < j \leq n+1\}$ in $\mathbb{R}^{n+1}$, projected to $\mathbb{R}^n$. For any triple of these vectors, the symmetry of the coordinate structure forces at least two equal distances.
mathContext: $f(n) \geq \binom{n+1}{2}$ [Alweiss]. Construction: $\{e_i + e_j : i < j\} \subset \mathbb{R}^{n+1}$, projected to an $n$-dimensional subspace. For $n = 4$: $\binom{5}{2} = 10$.

title: Weisenberg Improvement: $f(n) \geq \binom{n+1}{2} + 1$
content: Weisenberg showed that one additional point can always be added to Alweiss's $\{e_i + e_j\}$ construction while preserving the isosceles property, improving the lower bound by 1. The added point exploits the symmetry of the construction to maintain equal distances with all existing triples.

title: Combined Bounds: $\binom{n+1}{2}+1 \leq f(n) \leq \binom{n+2}{2}$
content: The theorem $\texttt{erdos\_503\_bounds}$ combines the Weisenberg lower bound and Blokhuis upper bound: for $n \geq 2$, $\binom{n+1}{2}+1 \leq f(n) \leq \binom{n+2}{2}$. The gap is $\binom{n+2}{2} - \binom{n+1}{2} - 1 = n$, growing linearly in $n$. This is the only proved theorem in the file (not axiomatized), following directly from the two axioms.
mathContext: $\binom{n+1}{2}+1 \leq f(n) \leq \binom{n+2}{2}$. Gap: $\binom{n+2}{2} - \binom{n+1}{2} = n+1$, so after the $+1$, the gap is $n$. For $n = 10$: $56 \leq f(10) \leq 66$.

title: Consistency Check: $n = 2$
content: Verifies $\binom{3}{2}+1 = 4 \leq 6 \leq \binom{4}{2} = 6$ by $\texttt{norm\_num}$. The Blokhuis upper bound is tight for $n = 2$: $f(2) = 6 = \binom{4}{2}$.
mathContext: $4 \leq 6 \leq 6$. Since $f(2) = \binom{4}{2}$, the upper bound is achieved. The lower bound $4 < 6$ shows Weisenberg is not tight for $n = 2$.

title: Consistency Check: $n = 3$
content: Verifies $\binom{4}{2}+1 = 7 \leq 8 \leq \binom{5}{2} = 10$ by $\texttt{norm\_num}$. Neither bound is tight for $n = 3$: $f(3) = 8$ with lower bound 7 and upper bound 10.
mathContext: $7 \leq 8 \leq 10$. Since $f(3) = 8 \neq 7 \neq 10$, both bounds are strict for $n = 3$. The Blokhuis bound has slack 2 and Weisenberg has slack 1.

title: Summary: Exact Values $f(2) = 6$, $f(3) = 8$
content: The summary theorem $\texttt{erdos\_503\_summary}$ records the two known exact values: $f(2) = 6$ (Kelly) and $f(3) = 8$ (Croft). These follow directly from the axioms $\texttt{kelly\_R2}$ and $\texttt{croft\_R3}$. The exact value of $f(n)$ for any $n \geq 4$ remains an open problem.
